name: Foreign missions convention
description: Baptist leaders organized a national missionary convention to coordinate foreign missions (the Triennial Convention).
narrative: Baptist leaders organized a national missionary convention to coordinate foreign missions (the Triennial Convention). Baptist support for overseas missions produced the General Missionary Convention in 1814, popularly called Triennial because of its meeting cycle. Mission societies coordinated work that individual autonomous congregations could not easily sustain alone. Conflict over appointing slaveholders as missionaries contributed to Southern Baptist organization in 1845. Northern mission societies later participated in the coordination established by the Northern Baptist Convention in 1907; that is a broader institutional history than a simple renaming of this convention.

key_figures.summary: An American missionary to Burma whose work helped mobilize Baptist foreign-missions support; he belongs to the missionary heritage rather than the 1907 founding generation.

name: Southern separation over slavery
description: Southern Baptists separated from the Triennial Convention in 1845 to uphold slavery.
narrative: Southern Baptists separated from the Triennial Convention in 1845 to uphold slavery. Southern organizers created a separate missionary convention after national mission agencies would not accept slaveholding missionary candidates. The convention developed common mission, educational, and publishing institutions while affirming local church autonomy. Its contemporary statement of faith defines a conservative evangelical identity. In 1995 the convention formally acknowledged slavery’s part in its origins and repented of racism; its founding context and subsequent self-examination both belong in the account.

name: Missionary heritage and northern coordination
description: Earlier Baptist missionary organizations supplied an institutional heritage for the Northern Baptist Convention organized in 1907. The American Baptist Churches USA name dates to 1972; this is not a direct 1907 renaming of the original Triennial Convention.
narrative: Earlier Baptist missionary organizations supplied an institutional heritage for the Northern Baptist Convention organized in 1907. The American Baptist Churches USA name dates to 1972; this is not a direct 1907 renaming of the original Triennial Convention. Northern Baptist churches coordinated mission societies through a convention organized in 1907. It became the American Baptist Convention in 1950 and American Baptist Churches USA in 1972. The present body maintains a connection to earlier missionary work without being simply the Triennial Convention under a new name. Its history includes both evangelistic mission and social service, with unity negotiated among churches that do not agree on every question.

name: Merger of conventions
description: NBCUSA formed in 1895 by merging multiple Baptist conventions.
narrative: NBCUSA formed in 1895 by merging multiple Baptist conventions. In 1895 earlier Black Baptist conventions united their mission and educational efforts. This organization grew in a society shaped by slavery’s aftermath and racial exclusion, creating institutions under Black leadership. Later disputes over the publishing board and over leadership and civil-rights strategy produced separate conventions. Organizational separation should not be mistaken for an entirely new theology each time.

name: Separation from NBCUSA
narrative: NBCA separated from NBCUSA in 1915. The National Baptist publishing-board controversy divided leaders who otherwise shared much Baptist theology. The National Baptist Convention of America developed as a separate cooperative body rather than as the result of a new doctrine of baptism or salvation. Its history is therefore best explained through institutional authority, publishing, and autonomous Black church cooperation, with attention to subsequent organizational changes that need further detailed research.

key_figures.role: publishing-board leader central to the institutional context of the 1915 dispute
key_figures.summary: Richard Henry Boyd was a Black Baptist publishing organizer whose struggle over publishing-board independence helped produce the 1915 convention division.

name: Separation from NBCUSA
narrative: PNBC separated from NBCUSA in 1961. The 1961 National Baptist Convention meeting exposed conflict over incumbent leadership and the use of nonviolent direct action. Ministers associated with Gardner Taylor and supporters of Martin Luther King Jr.’s approach formed a separate convention in Cincinnati that November. Its distinctive historical role is the institutional space it provided for civil-rights advocacy within a Baptist framework, rather than a wholly separate baptismal theology.

key_figures.summary: A Baptist preacher and leader in the 1961 opposition to J. H. Jackson, associated with the emerging Progressive National Baptist Convention.

key_figures.role: minister whose nonviolent activism was supported by the new convention
key_figures.summary: A Baptist minister and civil-rights leader whose support for nonviolent direct action was central to the conflict behind PNBC formation.

name: Conservative Baptist separation
description: Conservative Baptists organized in 1947 amid controversy within the Northern Baptist Convention, forming the Conservative Baptist Association of America (now Venture Church Network).
narrative: Conservative Baptists organized in 1947 amid controversy within the Northern Baptist Convention, forming the Conservative Baptist Association of America (now Venture Church Network). Conservative Baptists first established mission agencies and then, in 1947, a separate association of churches amid conflict over theological direction in northern Baptist institutions. The present Venture Church Network describes that separation as a defense of historic evangelical convictions. Its network structure aims to strengthen local churches without replacing their government; the account of the dispute is the organization’s own interpretation and should be read as such.

key_figures.name: B. Myron Cedarholm
key_figures.role: Early Conservative Baptist worker and national general director
key_figures.summary: A Baptist minister who began work with the new association in 1947 and served as its second national general director from 1950 to 1965. He later founded Maranatha; his departure shows that the association’s early leadership was not a uniform, unchanging bloc.
